newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania president to leave for United States.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania president to leave for United States.

text.p: Tanzania's president leaves for the United States on Tuesday night to address the U.N. General Assembly and press for a deal with the International Monetary Fund.

The foreign ministry said President Benjamin Mkapa would meet U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in New York and World Bank President James Wolfensohn and senior officials of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Washington.
A foreign ministry official said Mkapa's maiden speech to the U.N. General Assembly would focus on international economic relations, instability in central Africa and problems in Burundi.
Mkapa would return in time to host a visit by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher to Arusha, northern Tanzania, on October 11 and a summit on Burundi, where the army seized power on July 25.
Tanzania's relations with the World Bank and IMF have improved under Mkapa, who was elected last November, and the East African country is hoping for renewed balance of payments aid from donors.
Talks are underway with the IMF for an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) soft loan worth $234 million.
But minor sticking points need to be ironed out before it goes to the IMF board for approval in November, a western diplomat said.

"A worry that they will be looking at is the wage bill for July which exceeded that which was budgeted. Tanzania is going to Washington to present its solution to this," Charlotta Norrby, economist at the Swedish embassy, told Reuters.
Tanzania's July wage bill was around 10 percent higher than predicted, raising fears that government recurrent revenue spending could exceed targets set in its June budget.
Harmonising tariffs between the mainland and Indian Ocean island of Zanzibar, part of the Tanzanian union, is another outstanding issue.
Once an ESAF deal is signed, the World Bank would be in a position to advance loans of $100 million and the Paris Club of western donors is expected to approve debt relief amounting to $220 million.

Tanzania, one of the world's poorest nations with a per capita income of $180, is also indebted for $7 billion dollars with the central bank accountable for 98 percent, according to central bank figures.

IMF and World Bank officials have praised economic performance in Tanzania, where gross domestic product growth is put by the government at five percent this year and inflation at 18 percent in August after peaking at 42 percent in early 1995.
